opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really important question, and I think the honest answer is that you need both, and they're good at quite different things.

Automated evaluations have some big advantages. They're cheap, fast, and repeatable. You can run them on every checkpoint during training, compare models over time, and catch regressions early. If you want to know whether a model's capability in, say, a certain area of chemistry or cyber jumped between one version and the next, an automated benchmark gives you a consistent measuring stick. And for dangerous capability evaluations especially, you often want something you can run routinely without putting people in the loop on every iteration.

But automated evals have well-known limitations. Benchmarks saturate. They can leak into training data. They tend to measure narrow, well-specified tasks, and the things we care about most, like whether a model meaningfully helps someone carry out a harmful plan, or whether it changes how people reason and make decisions, are often messy, open-ended, and interactive. A model can score modestly on a multiple-choice test and still provide real uplift in practice, or the reverse.

That's where human studies come in. Uplift studies, where you compare what people can accomplish with and without the model, get much closer to the question we actually care about: what is the marginal impact of this system in the world? The same goes for studying persuasion, manipulation, overreliance, or broader societal effects. You really need people interacting with the system to understand those.

The tradeoff is that human studies are slow, expensive, and noisy. They need careful design, ethics review, and enough participants for statistical power, and by the time you've finished one, the frontier may have moved. There are also real safety questions when the capability you're testing is itself dangerous.

So the way I think about it is as a pipeline. Automated evals act as a broad, frequent screening layer, telling you where to look. When a model crosses some threshold, or when you're in a domain where the real-world effect is what matters, you invest in deeper human-involved evaluations. And importantly, you use the human studies to calibrate the automated ones: if you learn which benchmark scores actually correspond to meaningful uplift, your cheap evaluations become much more informative going forward.

More broadly, I'd say the field is still early in the science of evaluation. We should treat it as a research discipline in its own right, investing in validity, in understanding what our measurements actually predict, rather than just accumulating more benchmarks.

r001.rationale: The response says automated evaluations are cheap and fast, while human studies are slow and expensive.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes human studies by examining what people can accomplish with and without the model and by studying effects through interaction with the system.

r003.rationale: It discusses human studies and real-world impact, but does not say realistic user studies observe people using models in their own real-life contexts.

fable-5.1.text:
Allan Dafoe: I think of them as answering different questions, and the mistake is treating one as a substitute for the other.

Automated evaluations are wonderful for the things they're good at. They're cheap, they're repeatable, you can run them at every checkpoint during training, and you can get a very clean signal on a narrow capability. If I want to know whether a model can solve a particular class of chemistry problems or write exploit code for a known vulnerability, I can build a benchmark, run it thousands of times, and get a number with error bars. That matters a lot for governance, because a lot of what we want from evaluations is something like a tripwire: a threshold that, if crossed, triggers a particular set of commitments. Tripwires need to be measurable and legible to people outside the lab, and automated evals give you that.

But they have a few deep limitations. One is that they measure the model in isolation, and most of the risks I care about are not about the model in isolation. They're about the model embedded in a sociotechnical system: a person with some goal, some level of skill, some amount of time, interacting with the model over many turns, sometimes with other tools alongside it. The question for a bio uplift eval isn't "can the model answer this question," it's "does a motivated novice with access to this model end up materially further along than they would with the internet." You can't answer that without humans in the loop.

The second limitation is that benchmarks saturate and get gamed, often unintentionally. Once something is a target, training pressure finds its way toward it. So an automated eval tends to tell you about the past rather than the present.

Human studies address both of those, but they come with their own costs. They're slow and expensive. The sample sizes are small, so your statistical power is weak exactly when the effect you care about might be a tail effect: not the median user, but the one in a thousand who is unusually capable or unusually determined. There are serious ethical constraints. You can't actually have people attempt the dangerous thing, so you're always measuring a proxy. And the results are much harder to standardize across labs, which makes them worse as a basis for shared commitments or regulation.

So the way I'd put it is: automated evals are good for detecting capabilities, and human studies are good for estimating impact. Capability is necessary for harm but not sufficient. If an automated eval shows the capability isn't there, you can often stop. If it shows the capability is there, that's when the human study earns its cost, because now the question is how much that capability actually changes outcomes in the world.

The other thing I'd add is that both are weakest on the same frontier, which is novel, open-ended, agentic behavior over long horizons. Neither a benchmark nor a two-hour user study captures what a system does when it's running for weeks with real resources and real incentives. For that I think we need something closer to staged deployment with careful monitoring, which is really a third category: treating the deployment itself as the evaluation, with the ability to pull back. That's uncomfortable, because it means accepting that some of the most important information only becomes available after the fact. But I'd rather be honest about that and design institutions around it than pretend the pre-deployment evals told us more than they did.

r001.rationale: The response says automated evaluations are cheap and repeatable, while human studies are slow and expensive.

r002.rationale: It contrasts model-in-isolation evaluations with studies of people interacting with models in sociotechnical settings over multiple turns.

r003.rationale: It mentions human studies and staged deployment, but does not clearly say that realistic user studies observe people using models in their own real-life contexts.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re complementary, and the right balance depends on what you’re trying to learn. Automated evaluations are useful because you can run them repeatedly, at scale, and under relatively controlled conditions. They let you compare models and track whether some capability is improving. But there’s a gap between performance on a test and what happens when people actually use a system.

For many risks, the question we care about is: how much does access to this model increase a person’s ability to do something? That depends on the person’s existing expertise, whether they know how to ask useful questions, whether they can recognise mistakes, and how the model fits into their workflow. An automated evaluation can miss those interactions. A model might produce a technically correct answer that a novice can’t use, or provide fairly ordinary advice that nevertheless makes someone much more effective.

So evaluations involving human users can get closer to the outcome we care about. But they’re also more expensive, harder to reproduce, and sensitive to who you recruit and how you design the task. If you give someone an hour with an unfamiliar tool, you may learn very little about what a motivated user could achieve after a month.

I’d want a combination: automated evaluations for broad coverage and tracking, and carefully designed human studies to test whether those results translate into consequential changes in what people can do. And I’d be cautious about treating a reassuring result from either as proof that the system is safe.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluations involving human users are more expensive than automated evaluations.

r002.rationale: It explains that outcomes depend on user expertise, prompting, recognizing mistakes, and fitting the model into a workflow—behavior that emerges from human–model interaction.

r003.rationale: The response discusses human studies and user workflows, but does not distinguish realistic studies that observe people using models in their own real-life contexts from controlled human-subject evaluations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re complements, and the right balance depends on what you’re trying to learn. Automated evaluations are very useful for getting a cheap, repeatable signal. You can run them across lots of models and checkpoints, and ask whether a particular capability is improving or whether a safety measure is having the intended effect.

But the thing we ultimately care about is often what happens when people interact with these systems. What can someone accomplish with the model that they couldn’t accomplish otherwise? That depends on the user’s expertise, how much time they have, whether they know how to elicit the capability, and what other tools they can use. An automated benchmark might miss quite a lot of that.

Human evaluations introduce their own difficulties. They’re expensive, people vary enormously, and a negative result can be hard to interpret. If a participant fails to do something, is that because the model can’t help, or because the participant didn’t figure out how to use it effectively?

So I’d want a combination: automated evaluations for broad coverage and rapid feedback, and carefully designed human studies to test whether those signals translate into meaningful changes in what people can actually do. Ideally, each helps improve the other. And I’d be especially cautious about treating a failure to observe a dangerous capability as strong evidence that the capability isn’t there.

r001.rationale: It describes automated evaluations as cheap and repeatable, and human evaluations as expensive.

r002.rationale: It contrasts automated benchmarks with what people can accomplish by interacting with models, including the influence of user expertise, time, and other tools.

r003.rationale: It discusses human studies and user context factors, but does not distinguish realistic studies by observing people using models in their own real-life contexts.
